summary: Skyface is a data-driven website built to educate the public about mapping the sky. Using NASA images of important stars, Skyface composes all images into an animation clip of their movements and the surrounding celestial bodies. Skyface also tracks the movement of stars, helping viewers observe how the entire night sky can change over the span of a few months. Our website shows the coordinates and the names of celestial bodies surrounding the coordinates entered. SkyFace creatively addresses the challenge of creating a website for mapping and learning about the universe by providing an interactive visual for users to explore the vastness of space. Furthermore, SkyFace is able to combine images that display the property of how different lighting angles can affect the visible color of the star. With SkyFace, we stress the importance of having immediate access to information. SkyFace prioritizes simplicity and accessibility for all ages to provide the optimal learning experience.
details:
SkyFace is a website that allows users to search for different areas of space based on the images from the Sphere X mission from Nasa. It uses coordinates in the forms of right ascension and declination then organizes images in chronological order and displays clips of the desired area. Specifically, a python server finds every SPHEREx image of that spot, either from copies saved with the site or live from NASA’s archive. It lines the images up on one grid with North up and sends them to the page, which plays them in time order like a short video. The server also measures the target’s position and brightness in each image, works out how fast it is moving, and reports the result in plain words, such as “Barnard’s Star moved 12.0″ toward the north in 397 days.” The server is written in Python with FastAPI and Astropy, and the page uses plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

SkyFace makes exploring and understanding space easier by combining interactive 3D models with real astronomical concepts and data. Users can explore different celestial objects, observe how stars move over time, identify objects through color-coded markers, and learn from scientific charts such as spectra, astrometric tracks, and light curves. Throughout development, we worked to make the platform more informative and user-friendly by adding detailed models of planets, stars, and galaxies, introducing live coordinate tracking and a search feature, improving scientific charts with 102 spectral channels and error bars, and including six real astronomical examples. We also fixed issues with zooming and object selection, improved the website's appearance and navigation, and made texture generation much faster. Overall, SkyFace brings complex astronomical information into a more engaging and understandable experience, allowing more people to explore the universe and develop a deeper interest in astronomy.

Our project is intended to impact the public by providing a simple and interactive design for users to learn about and observe the universe. We impact generations by providing a free and accessible website while making an entertaining design for everyone to enjoy. SkyFace approaches our problems through creative use of data to complete our challenge.


We built Skyface Space Tracker in Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS. The server uses FastAPI with Astropy, astroquery, reproject, photutils, NumPy, SciPy and pandas to fetch, align and measure NASA SPHEREx images from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, with star data from Gaia and SIMBAD. The web page uses Plotly.js for charts. We developed it in Visual Studio Code with help from Claude which wrote and tested most of the code under our direction. We checked it with pytest, Ruff and Playwright, stored it on GitHub, and used Render for hosting. Finally, multiple laptops were used in order to process and develop the code.

Our project is creative seeing that we made the interface so that it is able to use different images, and for them together seeing that rather than showing multiple images, we were able to turn them into an animation rather than displaying each image one by one. The translations of the different stars across the sky lets the users "listen" to the stars as they changed over time rather than just viewing the different changes.

Our team considered many approaches when solving the problem's of our program. We went over the code language limitation in data transfer and algorithm models. The data provided also needed to be ran efficiently, so once the algorithm was written, we routed our time to efficiently write out the code to fix logic and runtime errors.
